claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy initially has an FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy may contain microsegregation and a fine-scale heterogeneous grain structure.
The as-built alloy may contain minor native oxides.
Elevated-temperature oxidizing or reducing gas exposure promotes selective oxidation or reduction at grain boundaries and microsegregated regions.
Selective interfacial reactions produce brittle oxides or nonpassivating reduced phases.
The resulting interfacial phases accumulate internal stresses that can trigger catastrophic failure.
Brittle, non-adherent oxide layers at grain boundaries and microsegregated regions act as stress concentrators.
Under oxidizing conditions, Cr, Al, and Ti form oxide phases at internal interfaces.
Growth and spallation of internal or interfacial oxides intensify stress and embrittle the alloy.
Under reducing conditions, inadequate protective-scale formation permits internal oxidation or phase instability at microstructural defects.
Internal oxidation or phase instability under reducing conditions lowers interfacial cohesion.
Higher oxygen partial pressure produces more pronounced oxide formation than the starting-state baseline.
Higher oxygen partial pressure causes greater embrittlement and earlier catastrophic failure than in the starting-state baseline.
Reducing atmospheres with inadequate passivation cause slower internal degradation but eventually lead to a failure route similar to that in oxidizing atmospheres.
Degradation, measured through mechanical-property loss and oxide characterization, depends clearly on the gas environment.
The as-fabricated baseline has uniform mechanical properties and minimal oxide formation.
The proposed governing mechanism applies over 700–900 °C, oxidizing or diluted-H2/Ar atmospheres, and exposure durations up to 500 hours.

contradictions.description: The reducing-atmosphere branch is described alternately as formation of reduced phases, inadequate passivation, and internal oxidation. The hypothesis does not explain how an explicitly reducing H2/Ar environment supplies sufficient oxygen for internal oxidation or how reduced phases relate to that oxidation pathway.
